newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica analysts say Taiwan chemical deal unlikely.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica analysts say Taiwan chemical deal unlikely.

text.p: Analysts said on Thursday they expected Taiwan to drop plans to invest in a $3.5 billion South African petrochemicals plant after Pretoria announced it was switching diplomatic ties to Beijing.
Most industry analysts questioned the wisdom of going ahead with the plant, which they said would be inappropriate given current market conditions.

Taiwan said on Thursday it would not encourage investment in South Africa after President Nelson Mandela's decision to ditch Taipei for Beijing and Taiwan's Tuntex Distinct Corp said it would follow its government's line.
The investment was first proposed by Taiwanese vice premier Hsu Li-teh during an official visit to South Africa in August.
Tuntex proposed an aromatics plant to produce polyester fibre for the textile industry in a 50-50 joint venture with the local petrochemical industry in South Africa's Eastern Cape province.
Several South African companies have been mentioned as potential consortium partners, including Polifin, Sasol, Sentrachem and AECI.

SBC Warburg Securities researcher Themi Themistocleous was sceptical that the plan was appropriate at present, as South Africa first needed to expand production of ethylene, an essential feedstock for the fast-growing plastics industry,
Local companies had not appeared keen on the project's timing, he said.
Output would have been exported at a time when the aromatics market was "very weak because a lot of capacity has come on stream in the Far East".
He said he believed that the project had been proposed largely as a political carrot to help keep South Africa in the fold of 30 countries which recognised Taipei.
Department of Trade and Industry chemicals sector director Dave Walwyn said business with Taiwan had a diplomatic element, but that had not motivated the proposal.

"It was always our understanding that there was a political component to this, but it was driven by commercial considerations. The private sector of Taiwan are not lackeys of the government," he said.

The project was under consideration by a consortium of private sector companies and parastatal interests, including the Industrial Development Corporation and the Central Energy Fund (CEF), which had asked for more details and were expected to decide on the project by next March.
The spokesman for the consortium, Howard Roberts of the CEF, said there had been "no political preconditions".
Chemical Marketing and Consulting Services managing director Henry Laing said the Taiwanese had put a great deal of work into the proposal.
"My feeling is that project would probably still carry on as an ongoing project in an evaluation phase, and if the potential returns looked good, they would go ahead."
He believed that South Africa had been chosen for strategic reasons, as Taiwan might have wanted the plant offshore to reduce the risks. -- Cape Town newsroom +27 21 25-2238
